your-companys-god-is-showing.title: Your Company's God is Showing
your-companys-god-is-showing.author: Nic Payne
your-companys-god-is-showing.summary: What do your everyday choices say matters most? Look at the pace, rewards and sacrifices people are asked to make—not just the purpose written on the wall.

you-have-a-culture-problem.title: You Have a Culture Problem
you-have-a-culture-problem.author: Nic Payne
you-have-a-culture-problem.summary: The original explanation of Cultural Orbital Mechanics: how identity, relationship and vision give rise to culture, and how that culture shapes us in return.

stop-chasing-psychological-safety.title: Stop Chasing Psychological Safety
stop-chasing-psychological-safety.author: Nic Payne
stop-chasing-psychological-safety.summary: One person sees a possibility; another sees the cost or difficulty. Before making either person the problem, find out what their contribution lets you see.

the-366-billion-failure-its-time.title: The $366 Billion Failure: It’s Time to Burn the Leadership Playbook
the-366-billion-failure-its-time.author: Nic Payne
the-366-billion-failure-its-time.summary: Work is already shaping people every day. This essay asks why more advice and training can leave the conditions doing that shaping untouched.

the-17-year-leadership-innovation.title: The 17-Year Leadership Innovation Drought: Why we're still Waiting for the Next Big Idea
the-17-year-leadership-innovation.author: Nic Payne
the-17-year-leadership-innovation.summary: A challenge to leadership ideas that change their names while keeping the same assumptions. Background for the question: what would a different starting point look like?

when-mattering-isnt-enough.title: When Mattering Isn’t Enough
when-mattering-isnt-enough.author: Nic Payne
when-mattering-isnt-enough.summary: Feeling valued matters. What happens next? An invitation to make room for people to grow—and to let them change us, too.

the-magic-of-mr-greenleaf-a-servant.title: The Magic of Mr. Greenleaf — A Servant Leader’s Guide to the Impossible
the-magic-of-mr-greenleaf-a-servant.author: Nic Payne
the-magic-of-mr-greenleaf-a-servant.summary: You can care deeply and still wear yourself out trying to hold everything together. What would it take for the organization to carry some of that weight?

the-hollow-crown-why-our-leadership.title: The Hollow Crown: Why Our Leadership Narratives Have Failed
the-hollow-crown-why-our-leadership.author: Nic Payne
the-hollow-crown-why-our-leadership.summary: What if trying harder to be a good leader cannot repair the place you work? A starting point for asking who we are becoming, and who we are becoming with.

the-lie-weve-normalized-leadership.title: The Lie We’ve Normalized: “Leadership Is Influencing Behavior”
the-lie-weve-normalized-leadership.author: Nic Payne
the-lie-weve-normalized-leadership.summary: What happens when leadership means getting people to behave the way we want? Nic offers a different starting point: conditions where people can become whole together.

the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.title: The Search For Unapologetic Impracticality In Leadership: Part III - How We Trained Ourselves to Mistake Certainty for Wisdom
the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.author: Nic Payne
the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.summary: Part III asks what our measures leave out. Useful when the numbers look tidy but something important about the people or the work is still missing.

the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.title: The Search For Unapologetic Impracticality In Leadership: Part II - The Seduction of Certainty
the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.author: Nic Payne
the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.summary: Part II explores why certainty feels so reassuring—and why a neat answer or a familiar method cannot do our thinking for us.

chapgpt-schools-me-on-leading-well.title: ChapGPT schools me on leading well
chapgpt-schools-me-on-leading-well.author: Nic Payne
chapgpt-schools-me-on-leading-well.summary: A short written reflection on meeting another person as a person, rather than a role or something to use. The linked post also contains a video.

the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.title: The Search For Unapologetic Impracticality In Leadership: Part I - What We Measure, And What It Hides
the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.author: Nic Payne
the-search-for-unapologetic-impracticali.summary: Part I asks what our fascination with tools and measurable results leaves out: who people become, how they relate, and how they learn to use their judgment.

why-work-cant-be-your-church.title: Why Work Can't Be Your Church
why-work-cant-be-your-church.author: Nic Payne
why-work-cant-be-your-church.summary: Work already shapes identity and meaning. This essay asks what organizations can responsibly make room for, and what one overburdened manager cannot provide alone.

do-your-replacement-a-favor.title: Do Your Replacement a Favor
do-your-replacement-a-favor.author: Nic Payne
do-your-replacement-a-favor.summary: Could someone else step into your work without inheriting a maze of private favours and heroic effort? Leave behind decisions and relationships people can understand and use.

culture-vulture.title: [C]ulture → [V]ulture
culture-vulture.author: Nic Payne
culture-vulture.summary: What does being here do to a person over time? Look at the work people live with: the hours, the responsibility, the room to grow and the pressure to stay quiet.

singer-boundaries.title: Shape Up — Chapter 3: Set Boundaries
singer-boundaries.author: Ryan Singer
singer-boundaries.summary: Ryan Singer shows how a time limit can help a team find a smaller useful solution. Read ‘Fixed time, variable scope’ in Shape Up.

singer-pitch.title: Shape Up — Chapter 6: Write the Pitch
singer-pitch.author: Ryan Singer
singer-pitch.summary: For a useful way to explain the problem and limit the investment, read Ryan Singer’s ‘Write the Pitch.’ Borrow the parts that help you describe this experiment.

dora-wip.title: Work in process limits
dora-wip.author: DORA / Google Cloud
dora-wip.summary: If the team is busy but little seems to finish, DORA’s guide can help you see hidden work and decide how much to start at once.

bain-rapid.title: RAPID® Decision Making
bain-rapid.author: Bain & Company
bain-rapid.summary: Bain’s RAPID framework distinguishes advice, required approval, the final decision, and the work afterward. Use it to check the roles you have written down with the people involved.

torres-assumptions.title: Assumption Testing: Everything You Need to Know to Get Started
torres-assumptions.author: Teresa Torres
torres-assumptions.summary: Teresa Torres shows how to turn ‘we need to learn more’ into a specific customer or engineering question you can check before funding the full build.

owasp-authorization.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
owasp-authorization.author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
owasp-authorization.summary: For the developer checking access: OWASP explains why signing in is not enough, and how to enforce the rules on each request.

metr-evidence-pair.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
metr-evidence-pair.author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud / METR
metr-evidence-pair.summary: METR’s 2026 update explains why measuring AI’s effect is harder than a headline suggests. Read it alongside the 2025 study, then ask how your task and team differ.

willison-red-green.title: Red/green TDD — Agentic Engineering Patterns
willison-red-green.author: Simon Willison
willison-red-green.summary: For a practical test-writing exercise, Simon Willison shows how to check that a test catches the missing behavior before asking an AI tool to implement it.

willison-lenny-podcast.title: An AI state of the union: We’ve passed the inflection point, dark factories are coming, and automation timelines | Simon Willison
willison-lenny-podcast.author: Lenny Rachitsky, interviewing Simon Willison
willison-lenny-podcast.summary: Prefer listening? Start at 1:08:21 for Simon Willison’s discussion of testing AI-written code. The written example above is free too.

marquet-competence-clarity.title: Control In An Emergency
marquet-competence-clarity.author: L. David Marquet
marquet-competence-clarity.kind: Author's Leadership Nudge transcript and embedded video
marquet-competence-clarity.summary: David Marquet connects greater authority with the knowledge and shared purpose people need to use it. Useful when discussing what would make this responsibility workable.

metr-2025.title: Early-2025 developer productivity study
metr-2025.author: METR
metr-2025.summary: Read with METR’s 2026 update. Results describe the developers, tasks, and tools studied, not a forecast for your team.

orbital.title: You Have a Culture Problem
orbital.author: Nic Payne
orbital.summary: The original explanation of Cultural Orbital Mechanics: how identity, relationship and vision give rise to culture, and how that culture shapes us in return.

hid.title: Holistic Impact Depth
hid.author: Nic Payne / Holistic Shaping
hid.summary: Use the tree and five areas of health to look at what everyday work is doing to people.

bowl.title: Leadership as bowl, water, and current
bowl.author: Nic Payne
bowl.summary: Attention gives shape to the space between people; each person brings an inner life; relationship changes everyone involved. Start at 4:19 for the metaphor or 13:45 for its synthesis.

bowl-synthesis.title: Leadership: participating and being changed
bowl-synthesis.author: Nic Payne
bowl-synthesis.summary: Attention gives shape to the space between people; each person brings an inner life; relationship changes everyone involved. Start at 4:19 for the metaphor or 13:45 for its synthesis.

note-c-220111507.title: The words we use for people
note-c-220111507.author: Nic Payne
note-c-220111507.summary: Language can conceal the people in a plan. Nic objects to inherited vocabulary that treats people as instruments.

note-c-216911020.title: The person you bring home
note-c-216911020.author: Nic Payne
note-c-216911020.summary: The person formed at work goes home to relationships beyond the workplace; human consequences do not stop at the office door.

note-c-212180715.title: Every leader needs contact lenses
note-c-212180715.author: Nic Payne
note-c-212180715.summary: A trusted colleague can help reveal assumptions because they see a situation through a different experience. Nic offers a practical perspective exercise.

note-c-210830269.title: A future you can imagine together
note-c-210830269.author: Nic Payne
note-c-210830269.summary: Notice the gap between present experience and a future you could want together. An ordinary hopeful opening can start a real vision conversation.

note-c-199735328.title: How culture gains its pull
note-c-199735328.author: Nic Payne
note-c-199735328.summary: The way we relate and help each other grow gives culture its pull. A short introduction to the orbital metaphor, with a link to the full article.

site-start.title: Start here: the Holistic Shaping map
site-start.author: Nic Payne / Rebel Leaders
site-start.summary: An introduction to identity, relationship, vision, culture, and the five areas of health.

site-shelf.title: Nic’s bookshelf
site-shelf.author: Nic Payne / Rebel Leaders
site-shelf.summary: Books and listening that have helped shape Nic’s thinking. This is a collection of recommendations; it does not make every book a source for these tools.

site-archives.title: More teaching from Nic
site-archives.author: Nic Payne / Rebel Leaders
site-archives.summary: Browse Nic’s essays, videos, and shorter conversations.

codex-mirror.title: The Mirror Move
codex-mirror.author: Nic Payne / Rebel Leaders
codex-mirror.summary: Before making your case, say what you understand and ask the other person to correct it. Use this when you keep talking past each other.

codex-clarity.title: Clarity Contract
codex-clarity.author: Nic Payne / Rebel Leaders
codex-clarity.summary: Compare what each person thinks you own, do not own, and share. A conversation aid for agreeing responsibility—not a legal contract or a substitute for required approval.

codex-recover.title: Recover After You Missed It
codex-recover.author: Nic Payne / Rebel Leaders
codex-recover.summary: If you have already missed a promise, name what happened, acknowledge the effect, and agree what people can expect next.

codex-ghost.title: Kill the Ghost Goal
codex-ghost.author: Nic Payne / Rebel Leaders
codex-ghost.summary: When a plan changes, make clear what no longer needs doing. Otherwise people can end up trying to deliver both the old plan and the new one.

notes.title: Two people are being shaped by this conversation.
notes.body: You may leave an AI discussion feeling heard, dismissed, more curious, or more certain that the other person is the problem. That matters beyond the next experiment. Ask what this repeated argument is teaching each of you about your place on the team.
notes.question: What would help both of you take part without having to defend your worth?

notes.title: Let their answer change the future.
notes.body: In Nic’s orbital model, vision grows through relationship. Bring your idea for what could be better and invite your colleague to change it. An invitation to help shape the future needs room for an answer you didn’t expect.
notes.question: Which part of your proposal are you willing to rethink together?

notes.title: Meet the person behind the position.
notes.body: Before opening the conversation, notice what you are listening for. Are you trying to catch a weak argument, or understand the person who has to live with this decision? Nic’s bowl metaphor starts with the attention we bring. You are part of the relationship being shaped, too.
notes.question: What might you hear if you stop preparing your reply for a moment?

notes.title: What will this way of working do to the team?
notes.body: Holistic Shaping asks what our way of working does to people. Here, look beyond the code: room to learn the craft, confidence to question a result, a real say in the plan, work people can stand behind, and time to recover. Faster output can hide costs in any of those places.
notes.question: What would you change so people become more capable rather than quietly carrying more?

notes.title: Make the investment explicit.
notes.body: Ryan Singer’s Shape Up separates the problem worth solving from the amount of time you are willing to invest. That distinction can help you describe this experiment. It does not turn an untested idea into an approved production change.
notes.question: What are you willing to spend to answer this question, including review?

notes.title: Keep the evidence in its setting.
notes.body: METR’s early-2025 study and its 2026 update show why an AI productivity headline needs context. Teams, tasks, tools, and the way work is selected matter. Use the studies to sharpen your questions; use your own records to decide what happened here.
notes.question: What did your comparison count, and whose work could it have missed?

notes.title: Keep what you learned together.
notes.body: Record the reason for continuing, changing, pausing, or stopping. Also ask what changed between you: can people raise a concern sooner, explain their judgment, or offer a better idea? Those experiences help shape the next conversation and, over time, what feels normal here.
notes.question: What should the next person be able to understand without repeating this argument?

notes.title: Notice what the pressure is doing between you.
notes.body: A promised date can turn someone into ‘the person who made the mess’ and someone else into ‘the person who always says no.’ Nic’s bowl metaphor asks us to notice how our attention shapes the conversation. Find out what the other person is carrying before deciding who they are.
notes.question: What have you stopped asking because you think you already know their answer?

notes.title: A smaller promise can protect more than the schedule.
notes.body: Look at the work behind each option. Does it depend on lost sleep, skipped learning, or people saying yes when they know the plan is wrong? Ask the team what a smaller, useful delivery would let them do well. Shape Up offers a practical way to explore a fixed time limit with room to change the work.
notes.question: Which option can people honestly stand behind and sustain?

notes.title: You can be useful without pretending to know.
notes.body: Nic’s writing on certainty asks whether our tools help us use our judgment or let us avoid it. A confidence label does not settle the question. Explain what has been checked, what remains unknown, and when you will have a better answer.
notes.question: What are you being tempted to make sound more certain than it is?

notes.title: What will happen the next time someone promises a date?
notes.body: If you keep repairing promises made without the team, the latest update may only get you through this week. In the orbital model, repeated experiences shape identity and relationships; the culture that emerges then makes those experiences feel normal. Agree how the next promise will be checked before it is made.
notes.question: What needs to change so honesty does not depend on one person being unusually brave?

notes.title: The new request is somebody’s problem, too.
notes.body: Ask what the customer meeting needs to accomplish. A request that sounds careless from your side may carry a commitment you have not heard about. Understanding that does not erase the team’s existing work. It gives you something real to work out together.
notes.question: What do they need to happen, and what have they not heard about your situation?

notes.title: Include the work nobody put on the list.
notes.body: DORA’s guide to work in process limits includes support and maintenance alongside planned work. Use that reminder when listing commitments. Starting more work can leave everything waiting; a full calendar alone does not tell you what the team can finish.
notes.question: What keeps interrupting the team but never appears in the plan?

notes.title: Who pays for the extra work?
notes.body: Look at the cost to people as well as the work. If the demo only fits because someone gives up evenings, swallows a concern, or loses the time they needed to learn, put that into the discussion. Ask the people affected. The cost does not disappear because the plan leaves it out.
notes.question: What would need to change for the team to do this without quietly paying for it themselves?
notes.quote: Does our pace grow or shrink people?

notes.title: The calculator cannot make the choice for you.
notes.body: Ten days of work plus two more days will not fit into ten available days. That helps reveal the conflict. It cannot decide whose promise matters most, whether the work is ready to start, or what repeated interruptions do to trust and concentration. Bring those questions into the decision.
notes.question: What matters here that the numbers do not show?

notes.title: What are these repeated emergencies teaching people?
notes.body: If the loudest request always wins, people may learn that careful planning and honest commitments count for little. Cultural Orbital Mechanics asks how that experience shapes relationships, identity, and the future people can imagine together. Try one agreed way to consider new work, then see what changes.
notes.question: Can people now raise a conflict early and take part in deciding what happens?

notes.title: You cannot carry every missing decision yourself.
notes.body: Nic’s Greenleaf essay asks what happens when good people are expected to make a broken arrangement work through personal sacrifice. If you must privately persuade three directors every time the plan changes, name that pattern. Your request can help everyone know how the next decision will be made.
notes.question: What currently depends on you absorbing a problem nobody has agreed to fix?
notes.quote: No one, no matter how well-intentioned, can out-serve a broken system.

notes.title: Separate advice, approval, and the final call.
notes.body: Bain’s RAPID framework distinguishes the person recommending a decision, people giving input, people whose agreement is required, the final decision maker, and those doing the work. Use that distinction to check your map with the people involved. Writing someone’s name in the Lab does not give them new authority.
notes.question: Have the people named here agreed that this is how the decision works?

notes.title: What does “owning it” do to a person here?
notes.body: Holistic Shaping asks how everyday arrangements help people grow or cause harm. Responsibility without a way to decide can teach someone to keep quiet, seek permission for everything, or cover the gap with longer hours. Describe what is happening and ask for a workable decision arrangement, with the support needed to use it.
notes.question: What would let you exercise judgment and learn, rather than merely carry the consequences?

notes.title: Make the arrangement usable without you.
notes.body: Write down which decision this covers, who answers, how soon, and what happens while people wait. Try it on the next real request and review it together. The aim is a way of working that another person could understand, not another private favour you must keep asking for.
notes.question: Could someone new use this agreement without knowing whom to approach behind the scenes?

notes.title: Notice whether people’s place in the work changes.
notes.body: A clear decision arrangement can change more than response times. People may become more willing to take responsibility, offer an idea, or admit what they do not know. In the orbital model, those experiences shape who people understand themselves to be and how they relate. Ask whether the new arrangement is doing that in practice.
notes.question: Are people gaining room to contribute, or has permission simply moved to a different person?

notes.title: Find out what their words mean to them.
notes.body: In Nic’s writing on shared language, a practical constraint can be a contribution to the idea. ‘Final requirements’ might mean Finance needs to know what funding would cover. Ask what decision the request serves before explaining your preferred way of working.
notes.question: What do they need to decide, and what would help them decide it?

notes.title: Stay curious when the wording irritates you.
notes.body: It is easy to hear a project word and prepare a lecture about Product. Notice the person using it. They have work, pressures, and responsibilities of their own. Nic’s bowl metaphor asks what kind of attention we bring to the relationship and whether we leave room to be changed by it.
notes.question: What might you understand if you let them finish explaining the request?

notes.title: Give uncertainty a useful next step.
notes.body: You can make a real commitment without promising an answer you do not yet have. Say which question you will check, how, and by when. Teresa Torres’s assumption-testing guide helps narrow that question. Nic’s writing on certainty explains why a polished plan should not replace judgment.
notes.question: Which belief must you check before asking people to commit to the whole build?

notes.title: Does your reply leave them able to participate?
notes.body: Consider what repeated exchanges like this do to people. A correction can leave someone embarrassed and less willing to ask. A clear explanation can help both of you learn the work, make better judgments, and build trust. Be specific about what you can offer, and invite them to tell you what is still missing.
notes.question: Can they question or change your proposal without being made to feel foolish?

notes.title: Build a shared way to ask and answer.
notes.body: After the immediate request, ask what you now understand about each other’s work. Keep the explanation and decision where the next person can find them. Cultural Orbital Mechanics helps trace how repeated encounters shape identity and relationship—and what becomes normal between teams.
notes.question: Will the next request be easier because of what you learned together?

notes.title: Read your reply out loud.
notes.body: Nic’s Note on the words we inherit asks us to notice when language hides the person. Name the customer waiting for a repair, the developer checking the change, and the colleague who needs a funding decision. If a sentence sounds like something nobody would say, rewrite it before sending.
notes.question: Could the person receiving this explain what you are offering and what you need from them?
notes.quote: To lead differently, we must learn to speak a different language.
